issue.issue_text: Whether the Land Customs Act, 1924 would apply to the Santhal Parganas on the ground that it is an existing law under Article 372 of the Constitution.

facts: The Santhal Parganas was an 'excluded or partially excluded area' under the Government of India Act, 1935.
Prior to the Constitution, laws like the Land Customs Act, 1924, did not automatically apply to these areas; they required a specific notification by the Governor to be put into force.
The Land Customs Act, 1924, had not been specifically made applicable to the Santhal Parganas before the Constitution came into effect.
law: Article 372(1) of the Constitution states that all 'laws in force' in the territory of India before the Constitution shall continue in force.
Explanation I to Article 372 clarifies that 'law in force' includes a law that existed but was not yet in operation in a particular area.
The Fifth Schedule of the Constitution deals with the administration of excluded and partially excluded areas.
application: The respondent argued that the Land Customs Act, 1924, was an 'existing law' for the territory of India and, under Article 372, it automatically became applicable to the Santhal Parganas after the Constitution commenced, as the old restrictions (like needing a Governor's notification) were no longer operative.
The Supreme Court rejected this interpretation. It reasoned that Article 372 and its Explanation I were designed to preserve the legal status quo as it existed before the Constitution.
The Court distinguished between laws that were in force in excluded areas and laws that were in force in the rest of India.

It held that Article 372 saves laws that were existing in territories *other than* excluded areas for those territories, and it saves laws that were existing in excluded areas *for those specific areas*.

Crucially, the Court determined that a law that was an 'existing law' for the rest of India did not automatically become an 'existing law' under Article 372 for an excluded area where it had never been applied.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that because the Land Customs Act, 1924, was not in force in the Santhal Parganas before the Constitution, it did not qualify as an 'existing law' for that specific area under Article 372. Therefore, the Act did not apply to the Santhal Parganas on this ground.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Bihar Regulation I of 1951 is in excess of the Governor's powers.

facts: The Governor of Bihar enacted Bihar Regulation I of 1951, which made the Imports and Exports Control Act, 1947, applicable to the Santhal Parganas.
The Santhal Parganas are a 'Scheduled Area' as defined under Article 244 and the Fifth Schedule of the Constitution.
The appellants challenged this regulation, arguing that it was an act in excess of the Governor's constitutional powers.
law: The Governor's power to legislate for Scheduled Areas is derived from Article 244 and, specifically, paragraph 5 of the Fifth Schedule to the Constitution.
Paragraph 5(2) of the Fifth Schedule grants the Governor the power to make regulations for the peace and good government of any Scheduled Area.
Paragraph 5(3) gives the Governor the power to repeal or amend any Act of Parliament or State Legislature that applies to the area.
The Court noted that Section 92 of the Government of India Act, 1935, which previously governed these areas, was repealed by Article 395 of the Constitution and is no longer in force.
application: The Court rejected the appellants' contention that the power to 'make regulations' does not include the power to 'apply' a law made by another legislature.

The Court reasoned that the power to make regulations is a full legislative power that embraces the utmost power to make laws. It stated, "Applying law to an area is making regulations which are laws."
It further held that the power to apply laws is inherent in the Governor's power to repeal or amend existing laws applicable to the area.

The Court also dismissed the argument that the regulation was a piece of delegated or conditional legislation. Instead, it found that the Governor was exercising a direct legislative function, similar to how Parliament can apply a law to a particular state.
The regulation was deemed a valid piece of legislation emanating from the Governor's plenary legislative authority.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the challenge, holding that the Bihar Regulation I of 1951 was not in excess of the Governor's powers. The Court affirmed that the Governor's authority under the Fifth Schedule to the Constitution is a complete legislative power that includes the ability to apply existing laws to a Scheduled Area.

issue.issue_text: Whether the power to make Regulations for Scheduled Areas includes the power to apply a law passed by another legislature.

facts: The case concerns the Governor's power to legislate for Scheduled Areas under Paragraph 5 of the Fifth Schedule to the Constitution.
The appellants challenged Bihar Regulation I of 1951, arguing that the Governor exceeded his powers by applying a law made by another legislature to a Scheduled Area (Santhal Parganas).

The appellants contended that the power to "make regulations" does not include the power to apply an existing law, unlike the more explicit powers granted to the Governor under the previous Government of India Act, 1935.
law: Paragraph 5(2) of the Fifth Schedule to the Constitution grants the Governor the power to "make regulations for the peace and good government" of any Scheduled Area.
Paragraph 5(3) of the Fifth Schedule grants the Governor the power to "repeal or amend any Act of Parliament or of the Legislature of the State or any existing law" applicable to the area.
The phrase "peace and good government" has been interpreted by courts to confer the widest possible power to legislate for the area in question.
application: The Court rejected the appellants' argument, stating that the power to make regulations is a comprehensive legislative power.

The Court held that "applying law to an area is making regulations which are laws." It described the application of laws as a recognized form of legislation, where a new law is made by incorporating or referencing an existing statute.

The Court reasoned that the power to apply laws is also inherent in the Governor's explicit power to repeal or amend existing laws. The greater power to repeal or amend an act naturally includes the power to apply it.

By interpreting the phrase "peace and good government" as conferring the "utmost power to make laws," the Court concluded that the Governor's authority was not limited and fully encompassed the ability to apply laws from other legislatures.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the challenge, holding that the Governor's power under the Fifth Schedule to make regulations for the peace and good government of a Scheduled Area is a plenary legislative power that includes the power to apply a law passed by another legislature. The Court found that applying a law is a form of making a law and is an inherent part of the broad legislative authority granted to the Governor.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Land Customs Act, 1924 would apply to the Santhal Parganas on the ground that it is an existing law under Article 372 of the Constitution.
appellant_arguments: The Land Customs Act, 1924 did not apply to the place of occurrence.
Laws that were existing in territories other than excluded or partially excluded areas would not automatically become existing law for those areas under Article 372.
respondent_arguments: The Land Customs Act, 1924 became applicable to excluded areas after the Constitution because it was an 'existing law' under Article 372.

The restriction under section 92 of the Government of India Act, 1935, which required a specific declaration from the Governor to apply legislation to these areas, was no longer operative after the Constitution.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Bihar Regulation I of 1951 is in excess of the Governor's powers.
appellant_arguments: The power to apply laws under the Fifth Schedule was synonymous with conditional legislation, implying the Governor's action was an improper exercise of power.
respondent_arguments: The Governor had full power to make regulations which are laws, and this was not a case of delegated or conditional legislation.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the power to make Regulations for Scheduled Areas includes the power to apply a law passed by another legislature.
appellant_arguments: The power to apply laws under the Fifth Schedule was argued to be synonymous with conditional legislation, suggesting the Governor could not simply apply a law from another legislature.
respondent_arguments: The Governor has full power to make regulations which are laws, and just as Parliament can enact that a piece of legislation will apply to a particular area, the Governor could do so by regulation.

cases.principle: When clauses of a former Act are incorporated into a subsequent Act, the legal effect is to write those sections into the new Act as if they had been originally enacted in it.

When a notification under one Act (e.g., Foreign Exchange Regulation Act) is deemed to be a notification under a specific section (s. 19) of another Act (e.g., Sea Customs Act), a contravention of that notification attracts each and every provision of the latter Act.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The Governor's authority to make regulations for areas under the Fifth Schedule is a full legislative power, not delegated or conditional, and includes the power to apply existing laws to those areas. An existing law under Article 372 that did not apply to an excluded area before the Constitution does not automatically apply to that area after the Constitution's commencement. When a statute incorporates another by reference, stating that 'all the provisions' of the earlier Act shall apply, the effect is to write the entire earlier Act into the new one as if it were enacted therein for the first time.
obiter: In view of the fact that in the present case the seized articles were removed by the accused it is unnecessary to deal any further with this aspect of the case because if any order were passed for return of the bags the order could not- be enforced.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: When a statute, such as the Imports and Exports Control Act, 1947, deems a violation of its orders to be a prohibition under a specific section (s. 19) of an earlier Act (the Sea Customs Act, 1878) and further states that 'all the provisions of that Act shall have effect accordingly,' it incorporates the entirety of the earlier Act. The legal effect is to write all the sections of the earlier Act into the new one, making all of its provisions, not just the specified section, fully operative and effective.
legal_tests_applied: Doctrine of Incorporation by Reference: The court applied the principle that when a later Act incorporates provisions from an earlier Act, it is as if those provisions were written into the new Act for the first time. The court cited Lord Esher M.R. in Re Wood's Estate: 'if some clauses of a former Act were brought into the subsequent Act the legal effect was to write those sections into the new Act Just as if they had been written in it with the pen'.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's argument that only section 19 of the Sea Customs Act, 1878 would apply was rejected because it would render the statutory words 'and all the provisions of that Act shall have effect' both 'otiose' and 'nugatory'.

The court rejected the appellant's contention that the Governor's power to apply laws under the Fifth Schedule was merely conditional legislation, finding it to be a full power to make regulations which are laws.

The court disagreed with the appellant's argument that the Governor could not simply apply a law from another legislature, holding that the power to make regulations for Scheduled Areas includes this authority.
why_respondent_won: The respondent's position was upheld because the plain language of the Imports and Exports Control Act, 1947 states that 'all the provisions' of the Sea Customs Act, 1878 shall have effect, and the court found it would be an error to hold otherwise.
The court accepted the respondent's argument that the Governor possessed full power to make regulations which are laws, and this was not a case of delegated or conditional legislation.

The court agreed with the respondent that just as Parliament can enact legislation for a particular area, the Governor could achieve the same result by regulation, including by applying a law passed by another legislature.
policy_considerations: The court's reasoning is based on the principle of statutory interpretation that legislative language must be given its full effect. To ignore the clear mandate that 'all the provisions of that Act shall have effect' would undermine the intent of the legislature.
